lessons.title: Common Pig Diseases and Symptoms
lessons.body:
As a pig farmer in Africa, you must know the common diseases that can wipe out your herd. The most deadly is African Swine Fever (ASF). There is no vaccine. Symptoms include high fever (41Â°C+), loss of appetite, red skin blotches on ears and belly, vomiting, diarrhea, and sudden death. If you see these, call a vet immediately. ASF spreads fast; cull and bury deep (2 meters) or burn. Another major killer is swine erysipelas. Look for diamond-shaped red patches on the skin, high fever (40-41Â°C), and stiff walking. It responds to penicillin (e.g., 1 ml per 10 kg body weight, injected into the muscle for 3 days).

Piglets often get colibacillosis (E. coli diarrhea) within the first week. Symptoms: watery yellow or white diarrhea, dehydration, and death within 2-3 days. Treat with oral electrolytes and antibiotics like neomycin (follow label). Prevent by ensuring clean farrowing pens and vaccinating sows before farrowing. Another common problem is pneumonia, caused by bacteria like Pasteurella or viruses. Signs: coughing, labored breathing, fever, and poor growth. Use antibiotics such as oxytetracycline (20 mg/kg body weight, injected daily for 3-5 days). Improve ventilation and reduce dust.

Parasites also cause disease. Mange (sarcoptic mange) makes pigs rub against walls, causing thick crusts on ears and flanks. Treat with ivermectin injection (1 ml per 33 kg body weight, under the skin). Roundworms cause pot-belly, coughing, and poor growth. Deworm every 3-4 months with fenbendazole or ivermectin in feed. Always check with your local vet or extension officer for correct dosages.

Early recognition saves money. Walk through your pens daily. Look for pigs that are separated from the group, not eating, or lying down more than usual. Check their eyes (discharge), nose (dry or runny), skin (redness, lumps), and feces (blood, mucus, worms). Record any changes. If more than 2 pigs show the same signs, isolate them and call a vet. Do not wait. In Africa, where veterinary services may be far, your daily observation is the first line of defense.

lessons.title: Vaccination Programs and Protocols
lessons.body:
Vaccines are cheap insurance against deadly diseases. In Africa, the most important vaccines for pigs are against swine erysipelas, classical swine fever (CSF), and foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) where available. African Swine Fever has no vaccine, so you must rely on biosecurity. Work with your vet to design a program based on local disease threats. A typical schedule: vaccinate piglets at 6-8 weeks against erysipelas and CSF. Give a booster 3-4 weeks later. Sows should be vaccinated 2-4 weeks before farrowing to pass immunity to piglets through colostrum.

Store vaccines in a refrigerator between 2Â°C and 8Â°C. Never freeze them unless the label says so. Use a cooler box with ice packs when transporting. Before injecting, check the expiry date and shake the bottle gently. Use a clean needle and syringe for each pig. For piglets, use a 20-gauge needle; for adult pigs, 16- or 18-gauge. Inject into the neck muscle behind the ear, not the ham. The correct dose is on the labelâusually 1-2 ml per pig. Do not inject into fat; you want the vaccine in the muscle.

Follow the cold chain strictly. If a vaccine gets warm, it loses potency. Discard opened bottles after 24 hours unless the label says otherwise. Never mix different vaccines in one syringe unless instructed. Record every vaccination: date, vaccine name, batch number, and pig ID. This helps if a disease breaks out. If you see swelling at the injection site, that's normal. But if a pig collapses or has difficulty breathing, it may be an allergic reactionâcall a vet immediately.

Vaccination alone is not enough. It must go with good nutrition, clean water, and reduced stress. Stressed pigs respond poorly to vaccines. So, handle pigs calmly, avoid mixing groups, and provide shade. In many African countries, government vets offer free or subsidized vaccines for CSF and erysipelas. Ask your local agriculture office. If you cannot afford all vaccines, prioritize breeding sows and piglets, as they are most vulnerable. A simple rule: vaccinate before disease strikes, not after.

lessons.title: Parasite Control and Deworming
lessons.body:
Parasites steal feed and cause disease. In pigs, the main internal parasites are roundworms (Ascaris suum), whipworms, and nodular worms. External parasites include mange mites and lice. A heavy worm burden can reduce growth by 20-30% and cause coughing, diarrhea, and pot-belly. You may see worms in feces or a dull, rough coat. Mange causes intense itching, crusty skin, and weight loss. Control starts with clean pens. Remove manure daily. Keep floors dryâparasite eggs need moisture. Provide a concrete floor if possible; dirt floors harbor worms.

Deworm regularly. For piglets, deworm at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, and 10 weeks of age. For adult pigs, deworm every 3-4 months. Use drugs like ivermectin (injection: 1 ml per 33 kg body weight under the skin) or fenbendazole (in feed: 5 mg per kg body weight for 3 days). Albendazole is also effective (10 mg/kg). Always follow label instructions. Rotate drugs to prevent resistance. If you use ivermectin, it also kills mange mites and lice. For mange only, you can use amitraz spray or dip, but follow safety precautions.

Treat the whole herd at once, not just sick pigs. Otherwise, untreated pigs reinfect the rest. Mark your calendar and deworm all pigs on the same day. After deworming, you may see worms in feces for a day or twoâthat's normal. Clean pens thoroughly after deworming to remove eggs. If you have a small herd (less than 10 pigs), you can deworm individually. For larger herds, mix dewormer into feed. Make sure each pig gets the right dose; dominant pigs may eat more. Divide pigs into groups by size and feed the medicated feed in troughs with enough space.

Prevent re-infection. Quarantine new pigs for 30 days and deworm them before mixing. Keep pigs off wet, muddy areas. Rotate pastures if you have them. Provide clean water and feed from troughs, not on the ground. Control flies and rats, which can carry parasite eggs. If you see persistent itching or weight loss after deworming, consult a vetâmaybe you have a resistant parasite. Regular deworming is one of the cheapest ways to improve pig health and profit.

lessons.title: Biosecurity Measures to Prevent Disease
lessons.body:
Biosecurity means keeping diseases out of your farm. In Africa, where African Swine Fever is rampant, it is your only defense. Start with a fence around your pig pen. A simple wire fence or wooden palisade works. Keep a footbath at the entrance with disinfectant (e.g., 2% caustic soda or commercial virkon). Change it weekly. Anyone entering must dip their boots. Do not allow visitors who own pigs or have visited other farms within 48 hours. If they must enter, provide clean boots and overalls. Never let them bring pork products onto the farm.

Quarantine all new pigs for at least 30 days. Keep them in a separate pen, far from your main herd. Feed and water them last. Wear separate boots and clothes. After 30 days, if they show no signs of disease, you can mix them. But before mixing, deworm and vaccinate them. If any pig dies during quarantine, burn or bury it deep (2 meters) and disinfect the area. Never sell or eat a pig that died suddenlyâit could be ASF.

Control traffic. Vehicles that transport pigs or feed can carry viruses. Load and unload pigs at the gate, not inside your farm. If a truck must enter, disinfect its wheels and chassis. Use your own vehicle if possible. Keep feed in a closed store; do not let rodents or birds contaminate it. Store feed on pallets, not on the floor. Clean water is criticalâuse a borehole or treated water. Do not let pigs drink from stagnant pools.

Maintain clean pens. Remove manure daily. Wash floors with water and disinfectant every week. Let pens dry before putting pigs back. Provide separate tools for each pen; do not share shovels or buckets between sick and healthy pigs. If you have a disease outbreak, cull sick pigs immediately. Disinfect the entire pen with 2% caustic soda or 1% formalin. Leave it empty for at least 2 weeks. Burn or bury all bedding and manure. Remember, ASF virus survives in dead pigs, pork products, and on boots for days. One mistake can kill your whole herd. So, be strict. No exceptions.

lessons.title: Recognizing and Treating Sick Pigs
lessons.body:
A sick pig costs you money, so act fast. Every morning, walk through your pens and look for these signs: a pig that doesn't come to feed, stands apart, lies down more than usual, or has a rough coat. Check its eyesâdischarge or redness. Check its noseâdry or runny. Check its skinâred patches, lumps, or crusts. Check its fecesâdiarrhea, blood, or worms. Check its breathingâcoughing or panting. Take its temperature with a digital thermometer (normal is 38.5-39.5Â°C). If it's above 40Â°C, it has a fever. Isolate any sick pig immediately in a hospital pen with clean bedding, easy access to water, and soft feed.

Treat based on symptoms. For fever and unknown cause, start with a broad-spectrum antibiotic like oxytetracycline (20 mg/kg body weight, injected into the neck muscle daily for 3-5 days). For diarrhea, give oral rehydration solution (1 teaspoon salt, 1 tablespoon sugar in 1 liter water) and an antibiotic like neomycin in water. For pneumonia, use tylosin or enrofloxacin (follow label). For wounds, clean with iodine and apply an antibiotic spray. Never use human antibiotics without vet adviceâdosages differ. Always complete the full course, even if the pig looks better after 2 days. Stopping early breeds resistant bacteria.

Supportive care matters. Provide fresh water with electrolytes. Offer soft, palatable feed like cooked maize porridge with some milk. Keep the pig warm and dry. Reduce stressâhandle gently. If the pig is not eating, you may need to force-feed with a syringe (10-20 ml of porridge every 4 hours). Record all treatments: date, drug, dose, and pig ID. If no improvement after 3 days, call a vet. Some diseases like ASF have no treatment; you must cull to save the rest. Know when to give up: if a pig is down, cannot stand, and has a high fever with skin blotches, it may be ASF. Do not sell or eat it. Bury deep.

Prevention is better than cure. Keep pens clean, provide good feed, and reduce overcrowding. A healthy pig rarely gets sick. But when it does, quick action saves money. Keep a basic medicine kit: thermometer, syringes, needles, antibiotics, dewormer, electrolytes, and disinfectant. Store in a cool, dry place. Check expiry dates monthly. Train yourself and your workers to spot signs early. In Africa, where vets may be far, your observation and first aid can mean the difference between one dead pig and a dead herd.

lessons.title: Working with Veterinarians and Diagnostic Labs
lessons.body:
You cannot do everything alone. A good veterinarian is your best partner. In Africa, find a vet through your local agriculture office, veterinary council, or farmers' cooperative. Establish a relationship before an emergency. Ask them to visit your farm at least twice a year for a health check. During the visit, they can take blood samples, check for parasites, and advise on vaccinations. Keep their phone number saved. When you call, be ready to describe symptoms clearly: how many pigs are sick, their ages, what you see (fever, diarrhea, skin patches), and what you have already tried. This helps them decide if they need to come or can prescribe over the phone.

Diagnostic labs are crucial for confirming diseases like ASF, CSF, and erysipelas. Your vet can collect samples: blood in EDTA tubes for viruses, swabs from noses or rectums, and pieces of tissue from dead pigs (liver, spleen, lymph nodes) in a clean plastic bag on ice. Never freeze fresh samples unless instructed. Send them to a government or private lab. In many countries, the national veterinary lab offers subsidized testing. Results may take 3-7 days. While waiting, isolate sick pigs and disinfect. Do not move pigs off the farm. If ASF is confirmed, you must cull all pigs and disinfect. The government may compensate you in some countries.

Work with your vet to create a herd health plan. This includes vaccination schedules, deworming dates, biosecurity protocols, and a list of emergency contacts. Review it every 6 months. If you have a disease outbreak, your vet can help you report it to authorities. In many African countries, ASF is a notifiable diseaseâyou must report it. Failure to report can lead to spread and legal penalties. Also, ask your vet about training opportunities. Many NGOs and government programs offer short courses on pig health. Attend them.

Finally, keep good records. Write down every treatment, vaccination, and vet visit. Note the date, drug, dose, and pig ID. This helps your vet see patterns and make better decisions. If you sell pigs, buyers may ask for health records. Good records also help you claim insurance or compensation. Remember, a vet is not just for emergenciesâthey are a teacher and advisor. Treat them with respect, pay them fairly, and follow their advice. A strong vet-farmer relationship leads to healthier pigs and better profits.

quiz.q: Which disease has no vaccine and requires culling to control?
quiz.explanation: African Swine Fever has no vaccine, so infected pigs must be culled and buried deep.

quiz.q: What is a common symptom of swine erysipelas?
options: A) Diamond-shaped red patches on skin
quiz.explanation: Swine erysipelas typically causes diamond-shaped red patches on the skin.

quiz.q: Which antibiotic is commonly used to treat pneumonia in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Oxytetracycline is a broad-spectrum antibiotic effective against pneumonia-causing bacteria.

quiz.q: How often should adult pigs be dewormed?
quiz.explanation: Adult pigs should be dewormed every 3-4 months to control internal parasites.

quiz.q: What is the correct storage temperature for vaccines?
quiz.explanation: Vaccines must be stored in a refrigerator between 2Â°C and 8Â°C to maintain potency.

quiz.q: Which parasite causes intense itching and crusty skin in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Mange mites burrow into the skin, causing intense itching and crusty lesions.

quiz.q: What is the first step when you see a sick pig?
options: B) Isolate it from the herd
quiz.explanation: Isolating a sick pig prevents the spread of disease to healthy pigs.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is commonly given to piglets at 6-8 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Swine erysipelas vaccine is typically given to piglets at 6-8 weeks of age.

quiz.q: What is the normal body temperature of a pig?
quiz.explanation: A healthy pig's normal temperature is between 38.5Â°C and 39.5Â°C.

quiz.q: Which disinfectant is recommended for footbaths in pig farms?
quiz.explanation: 2% caustic soda is a strong disinfectant effective against many pig pathogens.

quiz.q: How long should new pigs be quarantined before mixing with the herd?
quiz.explanation: A 30-day quarantine helps ensure new pigs are not carrying diseases.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of colibacillosis in piglets?
quiz.explanation: Colibacillosis causes watery yellow or white diarrhea in young piglets.

quiz.q: Which drug is used to treat both internal worms and mange?
quiz.explanation: Ivermectin is effective against both internal parasites and external mites.

quiz.q: What should you do with a pig that dies suddenly?
options: B) Bury it deep or burn it
C) Leave it in the pen
D) Feed it to other pigs
quiz.explanation: Sudden death may indicate ASF; deep burial or burning prevents disease spread.

quiz.q: Which of these is a biosecurity measure?
options: C) Using a footbath at entrance
quiz.explanation: A footbath disinfects boots and prevents pathogens from entering the farm.

quiz.q: What is the correct injection site for vaccines in pigs?
options: B) Neck muscle behind the ear
quiz.explanation: The neck muscle behind the ear is the recommended site for pig injections.

quiz.q: Which sample is best for diagnosing viral diseases like ASF?
quiz.explanation: Blood collected in EDTA tubes is used for PCR testing for viruses like ASF.

quiz.q: How often should you clean and disinfect pig pens?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning and disinfection helps control disease-causing organisms.

quiz.q: What is a sign of pneumonia in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Pneumonia causes coughing, difficulty breathing, and fever.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is given to sows before farrowing to protect piglets?
quiz.explanation: Vaccinating sows against erysipelas passes immunity to piglets via colostrum.

quiz.q: What is the first aid for a pig with diarrhea?
quiz.explanation: Oral rehydration solution replaces lost fluids and electrolytes.

quiz.q: Which parasite causes pot-belly and poor growth in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Roundworms (Ascaris suum) can cause pot-belly, coughing, and stunted growth.

quiz.q: What should you do if a pig has a fever above 40Â°C?
options: B) Isolate and call a vet
quiz.explanation: High fever indicates serious illness; isolate and seek veterinary advice.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a biosecurity practice?
options: C) Mixing sick and healthy pigs
quiz.explanation: Mixing sick and healthy pigs spreads disease, violating biosecurity.

quiz.q: What is the correct dose of ivermectin for a 33 kg pig?
quiz.explanation: Ivermectin is dosed at 1 ml per 33 kg body weight, injected under the skin.

quiz.q: Why should you complete the full course of antibiotics?
options: C) To make pigs grow faster
quiz.explanation: Stopping antibiotics early can lead to resistant bacteria.

quiz.q: Which disease is notifiable in many African countries?
quiz.explanation: ASF is a notifiable disease; outbreaks must be reported to authorities.

quiz.q: What should you record after vaccinating pigs?
options: A) Date, vaccine, batch number, pig ID
quiz.explanation: Detailed records help track vaccination history and manage herd health.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of African Swine Fever?
options: A) Red skin blotches on ears and belly
quiz.explanation: ASF causes red skin blotches, high fever, and sudden death.

quiz.q: How can you prevent parasites from re-infecting your pigs?
options: A) Deworm all pigs at once
quiz.explanation: Treating the whole herd simultaneously prevents untreated pigs from reinfecting others.
